input.vignette:
A 16-year-old female presents with a sore throat and breathing difficulties. She developed cough, congestion, runny nose, low-grade fever, and body aches two days ago. Today, her cough worsened and began producing yellow phlegm. She reports shortness of breath, and her mother noticed a “funny sound” with her breathing that started this afternoon. She has had reduced appetite and minimal fluid intake. She is fully vaccinated, including for Covid-19, and SARS-CoV-2 testing is negative.

On examination, her temperature is 39.0°C, heart rate is 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. She appears tired, anxious, and ill, with increased work of breathing. Examination reveals nasal congestion but no drooling. Audible inspiratory stridor and moderate intercostal retractions are noted, which do not improve with racemic epinephrine. Breath sounds are present bilaterally without wheezing or rales. The remainder of the physical exam is unremarkable.

Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for this patient’s condition?

Options:
A. Group A Streptococcus
B. Parainfluenza virus type 1
C. Haemophilus influenzae type b
D. Mycoplasma pneumoniae
E. Staphylococcus aureus
F. Adenovirus
G. Influenza A virus
H. Respiratory syncytial virus
I. Epstein-Barr virus
J. Corynebacterium diphtheriae

knowledge_chunks.title: Pediatrics_Nelson
knowledge_chunks.text: In general viral pneumonias are associated more often with cough, wheezing, or stridor; fever is less prominent than with bacterial pneumonia. Mucosal congestion and upper airway inflammation suggest a viral infection. Bacterial pneumonias typically are associated with higher fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, and auscultatory findings of lung consolidation. Atypical pneumonia in young infants is characterized by tachypnea, cough, crackles on auscultation, and concomitant (chlamydial) conjunctivitis (infants) may be present. Other signs of respiratory distress include nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal retractions, and grunting.

knowledge_chunks.title: Croup in children. > Differential Diagnosis
knowledge_chunks.text: Acute epiglottitis is rare due to vaccination against Haemophilus influenzae type B. The patient does not have a barking cough but has anxiety out of proportion to the degree of respiratory distress. Symptom onset is generally rapid; the child appears febrile and ill-appearing. Affected children prefer to sit upright in a tripod position, and cough is rare. The thumb sign due to a swollen epiglottis may be noted on a radiograph. A cough is highly sensitive and specific for croup, whereas drooling may indicate bacterial epiglottitis. Other symptoms include acute onset of dysphagia, odynophagia, high fever, and a muffled voice.[12]

knowledge_chunks.title: Antibiotics for sore throat. > Etiology
knowledge_chunks.text: Tonsillitis is primarily caused by infectious agents, with viral pathogens accounting for most cases (approximately 70%–95%).[5][6] Common viral etiologies include rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, coronavirus, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus, and human immunodeficiency virus.[9] These viruses manifest as part of broader upper respiratory tract infections, although systemic viruses like EBV may produce more severe or prolonged illness.[5][6]
